caption:
Federal agents arrested an OpenAI engineer accused of hiding a recording device in an executive conference room.
Prosecutors say his searches and a chatbot account tied to his spouse helped build the case.
He faces up to five years in prison if convicted. A detention hearing is set for October 19.

slides.headline: The FBI just arrested an OpenAI engineer for *bugging* the executive conference room

slides.heading: A *national security* case
paras: Federal agents arrested Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, a Saudi national and OpenAI engineer, on October 9. He made his first federal court appearance on Tuesday.
U.S. Attorney Craig Missakian said: "For us it is a matter of national security."

slides.heading: Tripped up by *prompts*
paras: Prosecutors say he used a work productivity tool to ask about OpenAI building addresses, meeting rooms, calendars and where leaders would be.
A chatbot account tied to his spouse allegedly asked how to "build a continuous audio recorder" and "encrypt the SD card."

slides.heading: Behind the *TV*
paras: The device was hidden in toilet paper behind a TV. Security footage allegedly shows him near the room on several dates, though he had no permission to enter.
On October 5, he allegedly looked behind the TV. That day, security found a second recorder in a bag he left in another room.

slides.heading: What he *faces*
paras: FBI Director Kash Patel said the aim was to "capture sensitive communications about the company's super intelligence technology."
If convicted, he faces up to five years in prison and a $250,000 fine. These are allegations, and a detention hearing is set for October 19.

slides.hook: Spying on AI labs is now an FBI priority. Follow to see how this case unfolds.
